nutrients.lowText: Your vitamin D is below today's target, and oily fish, eggs, fortified milk and some safe sun can help.

nutrients.notes: 1 µg = 40 IU. Adults over 70 need 20 µg (800 IU) a day. The 2024 Endocrine Society guideline says healthy adults aged 18 to 74 need no more than the daily amount. It also advises against routine blood tests for them. In VITAL, 2,000 IU a day did not lower cancer or heart disease. It hinted at fewer cancer deaths after the first 2 years, but this was not a main result. The drop in autoimmune disease was also clearer after the first 2 years. Take vitamin D daily, not in big doses. One 500,000 IU dose a year raised falls and fractures. A dose of 60,000 IU a month raised falls. A 2024 review of monthly high doses found no overall rise in falls, but its authors still did not recommend them. The safe limit is a daily average, so a weekly dose prescribed by a doctor will look high on the day it is taken. Blood levels below 30 nmol/L (12 ng/mL) are low. Levels of 50 nmol/L (20 ng/mL) or more are enough for most people. Levels above 125 nmol/L (50 ng/mL) may cause harm. People with obesity or darker skin may need more. People with sarcoidosis or other conditions that raise calcium should ask a doctor before taking vitamin D. UK advice is 10 µg a day, especially in autumn and winter.

nutrients.notes: A 2015 review of 13 studies, reported by NIH, found no clear memory or thinking benefit from choline supplements in healthy adults. Supplements usually contain 10 to 250 mg. Choline raises TMAO, which has been linked to heart disease, but large studies of choline intake found no link to heart disease.

EFSA has two limits: 10 mg a day for nicotinic acid and 900 mg a day for nicotinamide (niacinamide); EFSA set none for pregnancy or breastfeeding. Use 10 mg if the form is nicotinic acid or unknown, and 35 mg if it is nicotinamide. Limits do not apply to doctor-supervised treatment.

studyRange.goal: Preventing heart attacks and strokes with prescription nicotinic acid (no benefit found)
studyRange.evidenceWhy: Large trials found no fewer heart attacks, strokes or deaths, and more side effects.

keyStudies.title: Niacin in patients with low HDL cholesterol levels receiving intensive statin therapy (AIM-HIGH)
keyStudies.finding: Adding 1,500 to 2,000 mg slow-release niacin to a statin in 3,414 heart patients gave no fewer heart events; the trial stopped early.

keyStudies.title: Effects of extended-release niacin with laropiprant in high-risk patients (HPS2-THRIVE)
keyStudies.finding: 2 g a day (with an anti-flushing drug) in 25,673 people gave no fewer heart events, but more diabetes problems, bleeding, infections and stomach, muscle and skin problems.

keyStudies.title: Niacin for primary and secondary prevention of cardiovascular events
keyStudies.finding: 23 trials (39,195 people): no fewer deaths, heart attacks or strokes, and people were about twice as likely to stop due to side effects.

keyStudies.title: A Phase 3 Randomized Trial of Nicotinamide for Skin-Cancer Chemoprevention (ONTRAC)
keyStudies.finding: In 386 people with past skin cancers, nicotinamide 500 mg twice a day lowered new non-melanoma skin cancers by 23%; the effect ended when they stopped.

keyStudies.title: Definition of a tolerable upper intake level of niacin: a systematic review and meta-analysis of the dose-dependent effects of nicotinamide and nicotinic acid supplementation
keyStudies.finding: 47 studies: in healthy people, nicotinic acid caused major side effects below 1,000 mg a day; the authors think current limits may be cautious.

forms.notes: Nicotinamide does not cause flushing and has fewer side effects. Nicotinic acid causes flushing from about 30 to 50 mg; taking it with food helps. 'Flush-free' inositol hexanicotinate is absorbed about 30% less on average. Slow-release nicotinic acid is more likely to harm the liver. Nicotinamide riboside and NMN are not sold as niacin sources and are not counted here.

nutrients.lowText: Niacin is low on your meter today, but most people get plenty from foods like chicken, fish and peanuts.
nutrients.highText: Your niacin from supplements is near the safe limit, so don't add more today.
nutrients.notes: Never suggest high-dose niacin. Large trials (AIM-HIGH, HPS2-THRIVE) and a Cochrane review found no fewer heart attacks, strokes or deaths, and more side effects, including new diabetes, bleeding and infections; AIM-HIGH also saw more strokes from blocked arteries. The daily need (16 mg men, 14 mg women) is above EFSA's 10 mg limit for nicotinic acid, so do not fill this meter with nicotinic acid supplements. US adults average about 21 to 31 mg a day from food alone. Food values do not include tryptophan from protein. The skin cancer trial dose (1,000 mg nicotinamide a day) is a doctor-led treatment, far above the US limit.

nutrients.notes: Use EFSA's 12 mg a day as the cap. With average food intake (about 1.5 to 2 mg a day), that leaves about 10 mg for supplements. Australia's regulator says nerve damage cannot be ruled out below 50 mg a day, and France reported a likely case at 21 mg a day. Signs of too much B6 can look like signs of too little. Doses studied for morning sickness (30 to 75 mg) and PMS (up to 100 mg) are above the EFSA limit, so they must be doctor-led.

nutrients.notes: Iron is the nutrient where unneeded pills most often cause harm. The app should never suggest iron pills unless the user confirms a blood test (ferritin) and a doctor's advice; the meter should count food so users do not chase the target with pills. Men and women after menopause rarely need iron, and about a third of them with iron-deficiency anaemia have an underlying gut problem, so they need a doctor. A ferritin under 30 µg/L suggests low iron (ODS). About 1 in 10 white people carry the main haemochromatosis gene change. 25 to 35% of regular blood donors become iron deficient. Keep iron away from children. Empty stomach is best (food can cut absorption by up to 75%), but taking it with food is fine if it upsets the stomach. Vitamin C: ODS says it boosts plant-iron absorption, but a 2020 trial found no extra benefit with iron pills and the BSG 2021 guideline does not recommend adding it. The 2017 alternate-day study is in Lancet Haematology; the 2020 one is in Haematologica. Treatment usually continues about 3 months after blood counts recover. limitResearch.notes: US limit: 10 mg a day from food and supplements. Europe: 5 mg a day, set in 2003. In 2023 EFSA reviewed copper and set a safe daily intake of 0.07 mg per kg of body weight, which it says equals 5 mg for adults. EFSA said new upper limits by age group would follow, but its August 2025 summary still lists the 2003 limit. The 2003 limit was not applied to pregnancy or breastfeeding for lack of data, and EFSA's 2025 summary still lists those as not defined. But the 2023 review says pregnant and breastfeeding women are at no greater risk than other women. UK expert group (EVM, 2003): safe upper level of 10 mg a day. The app should use 5 mg.

keyStudies.title: A randomized, placebo-controlled, clinical trial of high-dose supplementation with vitamins C and E, beta carotene, and zinc for age-related macular degeneration and vision loss: AREDS report no. 8
keyStudies.finding: 3,640 people aged 55–80, about 6 years. Zinc 80 mg plus copper 2 mg, with antioxidants, lowered the risk of advanced macular degeneration. No serious side effects.

keyStudies.title: Spinal bone loss in postmenopausal women supplemented with calcium and trace minerals
keyStudies.finding: 59 women, 2 years. Calcium plus zinc, manganese and copper (2.5 mg) stopped spinal bone loss compared with placebo. Copper was not tested alone.

keyStudies.title: Intake of copper has no effect on cognition in patients with mild Alzheimer's disease: a pilot phase 2 clinical trial
keyStudies.finding: 68 people took 8 mg a day for 12 months. No effect on memory or thinking, good or bad.

keyStudies.title: Re-evaluation of the existing health-based guidance values for copper and exposure assessment from all sources (EFSA Scientific Committee)
keyStudies.finding: Set a safe daily intake of 0.07 mg per kg body weight (5 mg a day for adults). No copper build-up in the liver is expected at 5 mg a day.

interactions.action: Keep total zinc within its upper limit. If a doctor prescribes high-dose zinc, ask whether copper should be added and checked.

Liver failure was reported in one person after 30 mg a day for 2 years, then 60 mg a day. EFSA's adequate intake for adults (1.6 mg men, 1.3 mg women) is higher than the US RDA of 0.9 mg. In one study, 15% of 200 adults and children with coeliac disease had low copper.

nutrients.notes: What human studies show on hormones. In men, the one placebo-controlled trial on testosterone (19 bodybuilders, 2.5 mg a day for 7 weeks) showed no change in testosterone, muscle or strength. Two small studies without a placebo group gave 10 mg a day: one (8 men, 1 week) found free testosterone up and estrogen down; the other (healthy men, 4 weeks) found estrogen up and only a trend in testosterone, so the two disagree on estrogen. In women after menopause, adding 3 mg a day to a very low-boron diet raised estrogen and testosterone in one study of 12 women, but changed nothing in another 3-week study. A single 11.6 mg dose in 15 men did not change blood sugar, blood fats or clotting. Overall, there is no good evidence that boron raises testosterone in healthy men. limit.note: The safe amount depends on the form. Well-absorbed forms were only checked up to 10 mg a day.

limitResearch.notes: No official upper limit in the US or Europe. EFSA (2004) said normal food intakes of 20–50 mg a day are unlikely to cause harm. UK experts (EVM, 2003) set a safe upper level of 700 mg a day of silicon from supplements as silica (silicon dioxide), or 760 mg in total (often quoted as 1,500 mg, which is the weight of silicon dioxide, not silicon). Well-absorbed forms are different: EFSA has only checked choline-stabilised orthosilicic acid and monomethylsilanetriol at up to 10 mg a day (no concerns found at that level). Germany's risk assessment institute (BfR) suggests no more than 10 mg a day of these forms per product, 100 mg as silica gel and 350 mg as silicon dioxide. keyStudies.finding: 50 women with sun-damaged skin took 10 mg a day or placebo for 20 weeks. Smoother skin than placebo, and less brittle hair and nails than at the start.

keyStudies.title: Effect of oral intake of choline-stabilized orthosilicic acid on hair tensile strength and morphology in women with fine hair
keyStudies.finding: 48 women with fine hair took 10 mg a day or placebo for 9 months. Hair kept more of its strength than with placebo and got thicker.

keyStudies.title: The silicon supplement 'Monomethylsilanetriol' is safe and increases the body pool of silicon in healthy Pre-menopausal women
keyStudies.finding: 22 women, 10.5 mg a day for 4 weeks. Body silicon rose with no side effects.

keyStudies.finding: Absorption varies by form: monomethylsilanetriol and alcohol-free beer about 60–64%, green beans 44%, orthosilicic acid 43%, choline-stabilised orthosilicic acid 17%, bananas 4%, colloidal silica 1%.

nutrients.notes: Silicon is not proven to be an essential nutrient, and the US Institute of Medicine noted there is no justification for adding it to supplements. Silicon is cleared by the kidneys, and levels run higher in kidney failure.

nutrients.notes: Count supplements only toward warnings. Fish meals are encouraged: adults are advised at least 8 oz (about 225 g) of seafood a week, and 8–12 oz of lower-mercury fish in pregnancy. Doses above 1 g a day belong in doctor-led care; 4 g doses are prescription medicines. For pregnancy and breastfeeding EFSA adds 100–200 mg of DHA; the target here uses the lower end (350 mg). Do not use cod liver oil in pregnancy because it contains vitamin A.

nutrients.name: Collagen peptides
nutrients.unitNotes: Grams of collagen peptides (hydrolysed collagen) or gelatin. Undenatured type II collagen is a different product taken at about 40 mg; log it separately.

conversions.note: Unsweetened gelatin powder is about 86% protein (USDA).

meter.targetWhy: Optional and not needed by everyone; studies mostly used 2.5–15 g a day.

limit.infoText: More than 15 g a day is above the usual amount in studies. There is no set limit; keep it moderate.
limit.note: Most studies used 2.5–15 g a day. Gelatin raised urine oxalate: ask first if you have had kidney stones.

limitResearch.notes: No official upper limit. Most studies used 2.5–15 g a day; some exercise studies gave 30 g around training sessions. Gelatin at 5–10 g raised oxalate in the urine, which matters if you get kidney stones. Suggested app rule: gentle note above 15 g a day, and keep protocols at or below 15 g a day unless a professional advises more.

studyRange.goal: Skin (2.5–10 g a day for 8–12 weeks), joint comfort (about 10 g a day) and tendons with strength training (5–15 g a day, some with vitamin C about 1 hour before exercise). Some exercise studies gave 30 g around training sessions.
studyRange.evidenceWhy: Many small trials show benefits for skin, joint pain and tendons, but independent and high-quality skin trials found no clear effect.

keyStudies.title: Effects of Oral Collagen for Skin Anti-Aging: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

keyStudies.title: Effects of Collagen Supplements on Skin Aging: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
keyStudies.finding: In 23 trials, skin benefits showed up overall, but not in trials free of industry funding or in high-quality trials.

keyStudies.title: Effect of collagen supplementation on knee osteoarthritis: an updated systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
keyStudies.finding: In 11 trials (870 people), collagen eased knee pain and improved function.

keyStudies.title: Vitamin C-enriched gelatin supplementation before intermittent activity augments collagen synthesis
keyStudies.finding: 15 g of gelatin with vitamin C, 1 hour before short exercise, doubled a blood marker of collagen building (8 men).

keyStudies.title: The Collagen Synthesis Response to an Acute Bout of Resistance Exercise Is Greater when Ingesting 30 g Hydrolyzed Collagen Compared with 15 g and 0 g in Resistance-Trained Young Men
keyStudies.finding: 30 g of collagen with 50 mg vitamin C before squats raised the collagen-building marker more than 15 g or none (10 men).

keyStudies.title: Specific collagen peptides increase adaptions of patellar tendon morphology following 14-weeks of high-load resistance training: A randomized-controlled trial
keyStudies.finding: 5 g a day with 14 weeks of strength training grew the knee tendon more than training alone (50 men).

keyStudies.title: Hydrolysed Collagen Supplementation Enhances Patellar Tendon Adaptations to 12 Weeks' Resistance Training in Middle-Aged Men
keyStudies.finding: 30 g with vitamin C after training, twice a week for 12 weeks, made knee tendons thicker and stiffer in middle-aged men (20 men).

keyStudies.title: Collagen Peptide Supplementation Enhances Muscle-Tendon Stiffness and Explosive Strength: A 16-wk Randomized Controlled Trial
keyStudies.finding: 10 g a day for 16 weeks made the calf muscle and Achilles tendon stiffer in 50 young men who did not train.

keyStudies.title: Impact of Collagen Peptide Supplementation in Combination with Long-Term Physical Training on Strength, Musculotendinous Remodeling, Functional Recovery, and Body Composition in Healthy Adults: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis
keyStudies.finding: In 19 trials (768 people), collagen plus training gave small gains in lean mass, strength and tendon size, with low to very low certainty.

nutrients.unitNotes: Billions of live microbes (colony-forming units, CFU). Use the CFU at the end of shelf life and note the strain name. Some yeast products list milligrams; log the CFU if it is shown.

conversions.note: 1 billion CFU = 1,000,000,000 CFU.
1,000 million CFU = 1 billion CFU.

meter.targetWhy: Optional; effects depend on the strain and there is no daily amount everyone needs.

limit.note: Safety depends on your health more than the dose. Avoid if your immune system is weak, unless your doctor says so.

studyRange.evidenceWhy: Reviews show fewer antibiotic-related diarrhoea cases, but certainty is low to moderate and results depend on the strain.

keyStudies.title: Probiotics for the prevention of pediatric antibiotic-associated diarrhea

keyStudies.title: Probiotics for the Prevention of Antibiotic-associated Diarrhea in Adults: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Placebo-Controlled Trials

keyStudies.title: Probiotics for the prevention of Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea in adults and children

keyStudies.title: Systematic review with meta-analysis: Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG in the prevention of antibiotic-associated diarrhoea in children and adults
keyStudies.finding: This strain cut antibiotic diarrhoea from 22% to 12% overall; in adults alone the benefit was not clear.

keyStudies.title: Systematic review and meta-analysis of Saccharomyces boulardii in adult patients
keyStudies.finding: This yeast probiotic roughly halved antibiotic diarrhoea in adults.

keyStudies.title: Strain-Specificity and Disease-Specificity of Probiotic Efficacy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
keyStudies.finding: Across 228 trials, benefits depended on the exact strain and the health problem.

keyStudies.title: AGA Clinical Practice Guidelines on the Role of Probiotics in the Management of Gastrointestinal Disorders
keyStudies.finding: Suggests only certain strains to prevent a serious gut infection during antibiotics, and probiotics for IBS, Crohn's or colitis only in research studies.

keyStudies.title: Gut-microbiota-targeted diets modulate human immune status
keyStudies.finding: In 36 healthy adults, 10 weeks of more fermented foods raised gut microbe variety and lowered 19 inflammation markers.

separateFrom.what: antifungal medicines (for the yeast probiotic Saccharomyces boulardii)
separateFrom.why: Antifungals can make this yeast probiotic work less well. Take it at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after.

better: Named, studied strains such as Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG or Saccharomyces boulardii
Products that list CFU at the end of shelf life

nutrients.name: Fibre
nutrients.unitNotes: Grams of dietary fibre from food and from supplements such as psyllium.

conversions.note: 14 g of fibre per 1,000 kcal (IOM adequate intake).

meter.targetWhy: IOM adequate intake: 14 g per 1,000 kcal, so 38 g for men and 25 g for women up to age 50 (30 g and 21 g after 50).

limit.note: Build up slowly to avoid wind and bloating.

limitResearch.notes: No upper limit was found in the sources checked. EFSA (2010) set 25 g a day as adequate for normal bowel habits. studyRange.goal: Psyllium on top of food fibre: the FDA heart claim uses 7 g or more a day of soluble fibre from psyllium husk; trials used about 10 g of psyllium a day to lower LDL cholesterol and improve blood sugar in type 2 diabetes.
studyRange.evidenceWhy: Many trials and meta-analyses show psyllium lowers LDL cholesterol; blood sugar benefits are seen mainly in type 2 diabetes.

keyStudies.finding: Adequate intake is 38 g (men) and 25 g (women) a day up to age 50, then 30 g and 21 g; 28 g in pregnancy and 29 g when breastfeeding.

keyStudies.title: Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics: Health Implications of Dietary Fiber

keyStudies.finding: 7 g or more a day of soluble fibre from psyllium husk, in a diet low in saturated fat, may lower heart disease risk.

keyStudies.finding: In 28 trials, about 10 g of psyllium a day lowered LDL ('bad') cholesterol by 0.33 mmol/L.

keyStudies.finding: In 41 trials (2,049 adults), psyllium lowered LDL ('bad') and total cholesterol.

keyStudies.finding: 25 g of fibre a day is adequate for normal bowel habits in adults.

nutrients.name: Protein
nutrients.unitNotes: Grams of protein from all food and supplements, including protein powders and collagen. Targets depend on body weight (grams per kg).

conversions.note: Multiply by your own weight in kg; 70 kg is the reference man.
Multiply by your own weight in kg; 60 kg is the reference woman.
Food labels count 4 kcal per gram of protein.

meter.targetWhy: RDA is 0.8 g per kg a day (56 g at 70 kg, 48 g at 60 kg); 1.2–1.6 g per kg with strength training; 1.0–1.2 g per kg over 65.

rules.why: RDA 0.8 g per kg a day; 1.2–1.6 g per kg with strength training; 1.0–1.2 g per kg from 65. Kidney disease: ask your doctor.

limit.note: Kidney disease: no fixed number — ask your doctor or dietitian.

limitResearch.notes: EFSA (2012) found the data too limited to set an upper limit. It says intakes up to twice the reference (about 1.7 g per kg) are eaten by active adults and are safe. studyRange.goal: 1.2–1.6 g per kg of body weight a day with regular strength training, shown here in grams for a 70 kg adult (72–96 g at 60 kg). Gains in muscle and strength level off above about 1.6 g per kg.
studyRange.evidenceWhy: A meta-analysis of 49 trials found small but consistent gains in muscle and strength when protein was added to strength training.

keyStudies.finding: The RDA is 0.8 g per kg a day: 56 g for men, 46 g for women, and 71 g in pregnancy and breastfeeding.

keyStudies.finding: Adults over 65 should aim for at least 1.0–1.2 g per kg a day, more if active or ill, unless they have severe kidney disease.

nutrients.name: Carbohydrates
nutrients.unitNotes: Grams of total carbohydrate (starches, sugars and fibre) as shown on food labels.

conversions.note: Food labels count 4 kcal per gram of carbohydrate.
1% of a 2,000 kcal day is 20 kcal, which is 5 g of carbohydrate.

keyStudies.finding: Blood creatinine rose a little (about 0.13 mg/dL), but urea and kidney filtration did not change.

forms.notes: Monohydrate is the most studied form. Taking it with a meal that has carbs or protein may help muscles take up more. Creatine breaks down in liquids over time, so mix the powder just before you drink it.

nutrients.notes: Optional; show it as tracked, not as a meter. 3–5 g a day fills muscle stores in 3–4 weeks without loading. nutrients.name: Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10)
nutrients.unitNotes: Milligrams of CoQ10 from supplements (ubiquinone or ubiquinol). Food gives only a few milligrams a day and is not counted.

meter.targetWhy: Optional; the body makes its own, and studies mostly used 100–300 mg a day.

limit.infoText: Safety is best shown up to 1,200 mg a day.

limitResearch.notes: No official upper limit. A 2006 risk assessment found strong safety evidence up to 1,200 mg a day; higher doses (up to 3,000 mg) have been used without serious effects, but data above 1,200 mg are not enough to be sure. Stomach upset is more common at 200 mg a day or more. Suggested app rule: gentle note above 300 mg, warning above 1,200 mg.

studyRange.goal: Statin-related muscle aches (100–600 mg a day for 30–90 days) and heart failure as add-on care (300 mg a day, in three doses).
studyRange.evidenceWhy: Results for statin muscle aches are mixed; one heart failure trial was positive but needs confirming; it has no clear effect on blood pressure.

keyStudies.title: The effect of coenzyme Q10 on morbidity and mortality in chronic heart failure: results from Q-SYMBIO: a randomized double-blind trial
keyStudies.finding: 300 mg a day for 2 years, added to usual care, lowered major heart events (15% vs 26%) in 420 people with heart failure.

keyStudies.title: Coenzyme Q10 for heart failure
keyStudies.finding: CoQ10 probably lowers deaths and hospital stays in heart failure, but the evidence is limited and mostly from one trial.

keyStudies.title: Blood pressure lowering efficacy of coenzyme Q10 for primary hypertension
keyStudies.finding: CoQ10 had no clinically important effect on blood pressure.

keyStudies.title: Effects of Coenzyme Q10 on Statin-Induced Myopathy: An Updated Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
keyStudies.finding: In 12 trials (575 people), CoQ10 eased statin-related muscle pain, weakness and cramps.

keyStudies.title: Effect of Coenzyme Q10 on statin-associated myalgia and adherence to statin therapy: A systematic review and meta-analysis
keyStudies.finding: In 7 trials (321 people), CoQ10 did not ease statin muscle pain or help people stay on statins.

keyStudies.title: Effects of coenzyme Q10 on statin-induced myopathy: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
keyStudies.finding: CoQ10 had no significant effect on statin muscle pain.

keyStudies.title: Effects of coenzyme Q10 supplementation on myopathy in statin-treated patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis
keyStudies.finding: In 7 trials (389 people, 100–600 mg a day), CoQ10 modestly lowered statin muscle pain.

keyStudies.title: Risk assessment for coenzyme Q10 (Ubiquinone)
keyStudies.finding: Safety evidence is strong up to 1,200 mg a day; side effects were no more common at 1,200 mg than at 60 mg.

keyStudies.title: Effect of Coenzyme Q10 and Ginkgo biloba on warfarin dosage in patients on long-term warfarin treatment. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled cross-over trial
keyStudies.finding: 100 mg a day for 4 weeks did not change warfarin needs in 24 people.

better: Oil-based soft gels taken with a meal that contains fat
forms.notes: CoQ10 is absorbed best with fat; oil-based forms absorb better than dry powder. Less than 5% of a dose reaches the blood. Both ubiquinone and ubiquinol are sold; this review did not confirm that one works better.

interactions.effect: CoQ10 may weaken warfarin in some people; study results are mixed.
interactions.action: Don't start it without the doctor who manages your warfarin, and have your clotting test checked more often.

interactions.effect: CoQ10 may lower how much insulin you need.
interactions.action: Check your blood sugar more often and tell your doctor.

interactions.effect: Antioxidant supplements, including CoQ10, may not mix well with some cancer treatments.
interactions.action: Only take it during cancer treatment if your cancer team agrees.

interactions.effect: Statins lower CoQ10 levels in the blood; it's not clear this causes problems.
interactions.action: Keep taking your statin. Evidence that CoQ10 eases statin aches is mixed.

nutrients.name: Ashwagandha (root extract)
nutrients.unitNotes: Milligrams of ashwagandha root extract. Products differ in strength (often standardised to a % of withanolides). Whole root powder doses are much larger and should not be compared with extract doses.

meter.targetWhy: Optional; not needed by everyone, and there are safety concerns for some groups.

limit.note: Rare liver injury has been reported. Not in pregnancy. Restricted in some countries.

limitResearch.notes: No official upper limit, and Denmark's 2020 assessment found no safe intake level could be set. It seems well tolerated for up to about 3 months; long-term safety is unknown. Liver injury has been reported, usually 2–12 weeks after starting, in cases taking about 450–2,100 mg a day. Suggested app rule: never suggest more than 600 mg a day or use beyond 3 months without a doctor.

studyRange.goal: Stress, anxiety and sleep in adults, usually for 6–12 weeks. Benefits were larger at about 600 mg a day and for 8 weeks or more.
studyRange.evidenceWhy: Several small, short trials show less stress and anxiety and slightly better sleep, but study quality and results vary.

keyStudies.title: Ashwagandha: Fact Sheet for Health Professionals (NIH Office of Dietary Supplements)
keyStudies.finding: An expert taskforce suggests 300–600 mg a day of root extract for anxiety; it seems well tolerated for about 3 months, but long-term safety is unknown.

keyStudies.title: Effect of Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera) extract on sleep: A systematic review and meta-analysis
keyStudies.finding: In 5 trials (400 people), sleep improved slightly, more with 600 mg a day or more, 8 weeks or more, and in people with insomnia.

keyStudies.title: Effects of ashwagandha (Withania somnifera) on mental health in adults: A systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
keyStudies.finding: In 22 trials, ashwagandha lowered stress, anxiety and low-mood scores, but trials varied a lot.

keyStudies.title: Safety and efficacy of Withania somnifera for anxiety and insomnia: Systematic review and meta-analysis
keyStudies.finding: In 5 trials (254 people), anxiety scores and some sleep measures improved; larger trials are needed.

keyStudies.title: Dual impact of Ashwagandha: Significant cortisol reduction but no effects on perceived stress - A systematic review and meta-analysis
keyStudies.finding: Ashwagandha lowered the stress hormone cortisol, but people did not report feeling less stressed.

keyStudies.title: Efficacy and Safety of Ashwagandha Root Extract in Subclinical Hypothyroid Patients: A Double-Blind, Randomized Placebo-Controlled Trial
keyStudies.finding: 600 mg a day for 8 weeks raised thyroid hormone levels, showing it can change thyroid function.

better: Root extract (the form used in most trials)
forms.notes: Most trials used root extracts, often standardised to 5% withanolides. Leaf products raise more concern: India announced a ban on leaf use in 2026, which is being challenged in court. Products vary a lot in strength.

If yellow skin or eyes, itching, unusual tiredness or stomach pain appear, stop it and see a doctor. Rules differ by country: Denmark banned it in food supplements in 2023; France (2024) advises pregnant or breastfeeding women, under-18s, and people with thyroid or other hormone problems, liver or heart problems, or on calming medicines to avoid it; the Netherlands advises against it; Australia requires a pregnancy warning on some products; the UK is still reviewing it (a third draft statement was discussed in September 2026); and EU food agencies proposed an EU-wide review in 2024. Check local rules before selling it in a protocol.

nutrients.name: NMN (nicotinamide mononucleotide)
nutrients.unitNotes: Milligrams of NMN (beta-NMN) from supplements.

conversions.note: EFSA: 300 mg NMN provides about 109.7 mg nicotinamide.

meter.targetWhy: Optional; benefits in people are not proven and long-term safety is unknown.

limit.source: No limit set; EU (EFSA 2026) judged 300 mg a day safe
limit.infoText: EFSA judged up to 300 mg a day safe for adults (not in pregnancy or breastfeeding).
limit.note: Not counted toward the vitamin B3 meter.

limitResearch.notes: No official upper limit. EFSA (May 2026) judged 300 mg a day safe for adults, not including pregnant or breastfeeding women. That gives about 110 mg of nicotinamide, below EFSA's 900 mg nicotinamide limit but above the US 35 mg limit for supplemental niacin. Trials used 250–2,000 mg a day for up to 24 weeks without clear harm, but long-term safety is unknown. Suggested app rule: warn above 300 mg a day.

studyRange.goal: Raising blood NAD (a molecule cells use for energy), and possible effects on insulin sensitivity, walking distance and blood pressure in middle-aged and older adults, over 2–24 weeks. Some trials in reviews used up to 2,000 mg a day.
studyRange.evidenceWhy: Trials are small and short; reviews found no clear benefit for blood sugar, blood fats or muscle.

keyStudies.title: Nicotinamide mononucleotide increases muscle insulin sensitivity in prediabetic women
keyStudies.finding: 250 mg a day for 10 weeks improved muscle insulin sensitivity in postmenopausal women with prediabetes who were overweight.

keyStudies.title: The efficacy and safety of β-nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) supplementation in healthy middle-aged adults: a randomized, multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group, dose-dependent clinical trial
keyStudies.finding: 300–900 mg a day for 60 days raised blood NAD (a molecule cells use for energy) and walking distance, most at 600 mg, and was well tolerated.

keyStudies.title: Effects of Nicotinamide Mononucleotide on Glucose and Lipid Metabolism in Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Randomised Controlled Trials
keyStudies.finding: In 8 trials (250–2,000 mg a day, up to 12 weeks), NMN did not clearly improve blood sugar or blood fats.

keyStudies.title: The Effect of Nicotinamide Mononucleotide and Riboside on Skeletal Muscle Mass and Function: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
keyStudies.finding: NMN did not help keep muscle mass or strength in adults over 60.

keyStudies.title: Safety and Metabolism-Related Outcomes of Oral Nicotinamide Mononucleotide Supplementation in Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
keyStudies.finding: In 15 trials (250–2,000 mg a day, 2–24 weeks), side effects and liver tests did not rise; the lower blood pressure number fell slightly.

keyStudies.title: Safety of beta-nicotinamide mononucleotide (β-NMN) pursuant the regulation (EU) 2015/2283 and the bioavailability of nicotinamide from this source in the context of Directive 2002/46/EC
keyStudies.finding: EFSA judged 300 mg a day safe for adults, not including pregnant or breastfeeding women.

forms.notes: No form has been shown to work better. Beta-NMN is the form EFSA assessed.

interactions.effect: NMN releases nicotinamide: 300 mg gives about 110 mg.
interactions.action: It isn't counted on the vitamin B3 meter. If you also take vitamin B3, ask your doctor.

nutrients.notes: Optional; show it as tracked, not as a meter. Legal status varies. US: FDA said in November 2022 that NMN could not be sold as a supplement, then reversed this on 29 September 2025; makers still need a new dietary ingredient notification, and FDA did not judge its safety. EU: NMN is an unauthorised novel food and cannot be sold in foods or supplements; EFSA gave a positive safety opinion in May 2026, but no EU authorisation was found as of July 2026.
